prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Mary who mattered to me, gone or asleep among fruits, spilled in ash, in dust, I did not leave you. Even now I can't keep from composing you, limbs & blue cloak & soft hands. I sleep to the sound of your name, I say there is no Mary except the word Mary, no trace on the dust of my pillowslip. I only dream of your ankles brushed by dark violets, of honeybees above you murmuring into a crown. Antique queen, the night dreams on: here are the pears I have washed for you, here the heavy-winged doves, asleep by the hyacinths. Here I am, having bathed carefully in the syllables of your name, in the air and the sea of them, the sharp scent of their sea foam. What is the matter with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I look behind? I carried you a long way into my mirror, believing you would carry me back out. Mary, I am still for you, I am still a numbness for you.

Keywords: Mary, Even, Antique

outputs.L1: Mary, who mattered to me—gone now, or perhaps only sleeping among the fruits, scattered in ash, in dust—I have not left you. Even now I cannot help but compose you: your limbs, your blue cloak, your soft hands. I sleep to the sound of your name, telling myself there is no Mary but the word *Mary*, no trace of you left in the dust upon my pillowslip. Yet still I dream—only of your ankles brushed by dark violets, of honeybees hovering above you, murmuring into a crown. Ancient queen, the night dreams on: here are the pears I have washed for you, here the heavy-winged doves, asleep among the hyacinths. Here I am, having bathed slowly in the syllables of your name, in their air and their sea, in the sharp scent of their foam. What is wrong with me? Mary, what word, what dust can I search behind? I carried you far into my mirror, believing you would carry me back out again. Mary, I remain still for you—I remain a numbness for you.
outputs.L2: Mary, you who once held meaning for me, whether vanished or slumbering among the fruit, scattered into ash and dust—I never abandoned you. Still, I cannot stop myself from shaping you anew: your limbs, your azure mantle, your gentle hands. Your name lulls me into sleep each night; I tell myself Mary exists only as sound, as language, leaving no imprint in the dust that gathers on my pillow. All I have are visions of your ankles grazed by dark blossoms, of bees droning above you as they weave a crown. Ancient sovereign, the darkness continues its dreaming: these are the pears I've cleaned for your sake, these the doves with their weighted wings, resting near the hyacinths. I stand here, having immersed myself thoroughly in the letters of your name, in their breath and their ocean, in the piercing salt-scent of their foam. What ails me so? Mary—what syllable, what remnant of dust might I search beneath? I bore you deep into the depths of my reflection, trusting you might lead me back to the surface. Mary, I remain devoted to you, frozen in stillness, numb on your behalf.
outputs.L3:
# On the Persistence of Mary

I never left her. This must be understood above all else—even now, when she exists as nothing more than ash scattered by some indifferent wind, dust settling on surfaces no one thinks to clean, a memory that grows thinner each year like paper held too long to light. I did not turn away. I did not forget. The abandonment others might perceive is illusion; I remained, I remain, faithful to something that may no longer have any right to be called a person at all.

And yet I know—I know—that "Mary" might be only a word now. Four letters arranged in a particular order, a sound the mouth makes, a shape the mind conjures without any corresponding flesh, without bone or breath or the particular way light once fell across an actual face. She may be nothing but language, a linguistic ghost with no material anchor, no trace in the physical world beyond this stubborn insistence of mine that she still means something. Even knowing this, even admitting the emptiness at the center of the name, I cannot stop myself from imagining her. I recreate her constantly, obsessively, the way one returns to a wound to check if it still hurts. Each recreation is both an act of love and a small betrayal of the truth.

So I bring her offerings, as though she were still capable of receiving them. Pears, heavy and golden, placed before an altar that exists only in the architecture of longing. Doves released into whatever sky she now inhabits, if she inhabits any sky at all. Hyacinths for the grief that never fully drains away, violets for the modesty of memory, honeybees humming their small devotions around a form that may be nothing but air. These are not rational gifts. They are ritual, sacred in their uselessness, offered to a figure who exists somewhere between dream and doctrine, between the woman she was and the icon I have made of her.

When I say her name, something happens that I cannot fully explain. The syllables become more than sound—they become immersion, a kind of baptism I perform on myself each time I speak them. To say "Mary" is to bathe in her, to be momentarily submerged in whatever she has become. The boundary between language and presence dissolves in these moments. I am not merely speaking about her; I am, however briefly, with her, inside the word that contains what's left of everything she was.

But this communion is one-directional, and I know it. I carry her with me into the mirrored rooms of my own interior world, into the hall of reflections where I have preserved her, multiplied her, kept her safe from the erasure that time insists upon. Yet she does not carry me back. There is no reciprocity in this haunting. I bring her into my private architecture of memory and longing, and there I remain, suspended, unable to move forward, unable to fully release her, unable to be returned to the ordinary world where such devotions might finally end. The longing persists, unresolved, and I persist with it—paralyzed, faithful, alone with the word that used to be a woman.
outputs.L4:
# Mary, In Absentia

I say your name the way one says a prayer
learned too late to save anything—
Mary, Mary, syllables like small stones
dropped into a well I can no longer hear the bottom of.

I have built you again tonight.
Out of habit. Out of hunger.
I have placed white flowers in your open hands—
gardenias, because you loved what bruised easily,
what browned at the edges within a day of touching.
I have set a bowl of fruit beside you: plums,
their skins so dark they look black in this light,
figs split open to show their red interiors,
because you told me once that opening things
was the only honesty you trusted.

Doves at the window. I put them there.
Two, because you said one was a widow-bird
and you refused to be anyone's metaphor
for loneliness, even then, even as you were becoming one.

This is not you. I know this is not you.
This is paper and breath and the old trick
of grief—how it borrows the shape of a face
and calls the borrowing a visitation.

I say Mary and my mouth remembers
the way it used to say your name
when you were still a body that could hear it,
still a weight the air had to move around.
Now the air moves through where you were
as if you were only ever an idea
the world was trying out, then abandoning.

I keep conjuring. This is my devotion:
to build the room again, the fruit, the flowers,
the two doves murmuring their soft, indifferent grief—
and to sit inside that room, waiting
for you to become real
the way saying *water* enough times
does not make the throat less dry.

I am learning what the word cannot do.
It cannot lift the stone. It cannot walk
you back through any door.
It only stands here, faithful and useless,
a small altar made of sound,
while I go numb in the posture of prayer,
hands open, holding nothing,
calling it your name.

There is a mirror in this kind of mourning.
I look into the invocation
and see only my own face
looking for yours behind it—
and behind that face, another,
and behind that, the same absence
wearing my devotion like a mask.

Mary. I have said it so many times tonight
it has stopped meaning you.
It is only sound now. Only shape.
The doves have gone quiet at the window.
The fruit will rot by morning.
And I will still be here,
mouthing the letters of a name
that no longer opens any door—
only this room, only this echo,
only the terrible, tender fact
of my own asking.
outputs.L5:
# The Antique Shop on Elm Street

Mary had always loved antiques, but there was something even more special about the old shop on Elm Street. Every Saturday morning, she would walk down the cobblestone path, past the bakery and the flower stand, until she reached the weathered wooden door with its brass handle worn smooth by decades of visitors.

The shop's owner, an elderly man named Mr. Whitfield, knew Mary by name. He would greet her with a warm smile, even before she stepped fully through the doorway. "Back again, Mary?" he'd ask, though he already knew the answer.

Inside, the shop was a treasure trove of forgotten stories. Ornate mirrors leaned against walls, their silver backing spotted with age. Porcelain dolls sat on shelves, their glass eyes watching visitors with quiet curiosity. Even the dust seemed to have character here, settling gently on stacks of yellowed books and tarnished silverware.

One afternoon, Mary discovered something extraordinary tucked away in a corner cabinet—a small wooden music box with intricate carvings of birds and vines. Even Mr. Whitfield seemed surprised, admitting he had forgotten it was even there. When Mary wound the tiny key, a delicate melody filled the air, notes that seemed to carry whispers of another era.

"This one has quite a history," Mr. Whitfield said, his voice softening. "It belonged to a young woman who traveled across the ocean with nothing but this box and a suitcase full of dreams."

Mary purchased the music box that day, understanding even then that some antiques aren't just objects—they're vessels carrying pieces of the past into the present, waiting patiently for someone to listen to their stories.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, elegiac free verse poem addressed to a woman named Mary, blending religious imagery (Madonna-like) with dreams, fruit, flowers, and dust.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Mary, Who Is Dust and Was Once a Garden**

Mary, I have seen you in the orchard of my sleeping,
your blue robe unstitching itself into evening,
each thread a swallow flying backward into the mouth of God.

You are always almost speaking.
The angel's dust still settles on your shoulder—
gold going gray, gray going nowhere,
a halo dimming like a bruise beneath the skin of the sky.

I remember the pomegranate you carried
though no one asked you to carry it,
how its red heart opened like a small wound
practicing the shape of birth, or grief,
I could never tell which
in the logic of the dream.

Your hands were always full of falling things—
figs gone soft with waiting,
lilies that forgot their whiteness
and turned the color of old prayer,
petals drifting down like the ash of something once alive,
something that had a name once,
maybe yours, maybe mine.

Mary, the dust remembers you
the way an empty room remembers a bell—
not the sound, but the shape the silence makes after.

I have walked through fields that were your face,
have eaten fruit that tasted of your name
and been unable to swallow,
my throat closing like a door in an old house
where no one lives, where someone always lived.

You are the mother of every orchard I have lost.
You are the seed that would not stay a seed.
You are the woman standing in the doorway of my dreaming,
holding out an apple that is also a wound,
a wound that is also a flower,
a flower that is also the dust
we all become, eventually,
softly,
without any angel to announce it.

Mary, I would light a candle for you
but the wax keeps turning into petals,
the flame keeps turning into birds,
and you—
you keep turning into the distance
between what I remember
and what was never true.

Still, I say your name
the way one says a prayer
to no one,
to everyone,
to the dust that was once a woman
who was once a garden
who is now only this:
a blessing I can't stop giving
to the emptiness
that answers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the style of grief and obsession, where the speaker mourns and idolizes someone named Mary, using repetition of her name and sensory imagery like violets, doves, and pears.
counterfactuals.output:
# Mary, In Fragments

Mary. Say it once and it's a prayer. Say it twice and it's a wound that won't close. Mary, Mary—I have worn your name smooth as a stone kept in the pocket, rubbed raw against my thumb until it forgets it was ever a word and becomes instead a kind of breathing.

There were violets that spring, do you remember, or am I the only one who remembers, am I the only room left where that spring still happens—their small bruised faces turned up along the fence, and you knelt to smell them though you always said violets have no scent worth kneeling for, and knelt anyway, because I asked, because I would have asked you to kneel for anything, for nothing, for the sake of watching your neck bend.

Mary of the doves. Mary of the gray wings clattering up from the eaves each dusk like something startled out of prayer. I have stood in that same yard a hundred evenings since, waiting for the sound, thinking each flutter might be you coming back wearing feathers instead of skin, thinking grief might be only a costume you shrugged into and could shrug back out of, if I called long enough, if I called correctly, Mary, Mary, the word going up into the dark like something released and never returning.

There were pears on the table the last October. You peeled one slow, the whole fruit unraveling in a single spiral, and you laughed at my astonishment as though patience were nothing, as though the world hadn't already begun taking you in small increments, membrane by membrane, and I ate what you handed me and did not taste it, too busy watching your mouth to notice my own.

I have made a religion of you. I know this. I have built the whole cathedral out of doves and violets and the pale wet flesh of pears, out of your name repeated until it loses meaning and becomes pure sound, pure ache, Mary Mary Mary—a bell that only tolls backward, calling not the living to worship but the dead to explain themselves.

Come back. Not as memory. Not as the smell of violets after rain or the sound of wings I mistake for your footstep on the porch. Come back as yourself, unbearable and specific, peeling fruit at my table, impatient with my grief, telling me to stop now, stop already, that you were never a saint, only a woman who liked the taste of pears and the hush of birds at evening—

but you don't come back.

Only the violets do, each spring, insistent and small and indifferent to the shape of my mourning. Only the doves, who have no memory of you, who startle up from the eaves for reasons that have nothing to do with grief. Only the pears, rotting sweetly in their bowl, going soft the way all soft things go, the way you went, the way I am going too, Mary, calling your name into rooms that have long since stopped answering.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of lyrical, stream-of-consciousness poetry about longing for a lost or dead woman named Mary, incorporating themes of memory, dust, mirrors, and the inadequacy of language.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Mirror Kept

Mary, I am saying your name again
into a room that does not answer,
the syllables falling like dust
falling the way dust falls
when no one is there to call it beautiful
or terrible or anything at all—
just motes, just the slow snow of what we shed,
skin cells and dead light,
the residue of a body that was once
so specifically yours: the wrist-bone,
the way you'd tuck the word *tomorrow*
into the corner of your mouth
like a secret you were saving.

I keep finding you in the mirror's argument—
how it holds a face and calls it *here*
when here has already gone,
how the glass keeps insisting
on a Mary who will not startle,
will not turn, will not
require anything of me
but this looking, this looking,
this terrible fidelity to a surface.

Language, that thin coin,
that counterfeit I keep trying to spend—
I say *loss* and it buys nothing,
I say *love* and the word
comes back smaller than I gave it,
diminished by the giving,
the way dust is smaller than the thing
it used to be a part of,
the chair, the book, the shoulder
you leaned your whole quiet weight against.

Mary—not the sound of you,
never the sound, only
the shape the sound leaves
in the dark after it's spoken,
a kind of afterimage,
the way you'd stare too long at a window
and then close your eyes
and the window was still there,
burned into the black,
persistent, false, exact.

Dust on the piano lid.
Dust in the seam of the closed book.
Dust like a soft language
spoken only by rooms,
by the objects that outlast us,
patient, indifferent, gathering—

and somewhere in that gathering,
some grammar I can't translate,
you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an intense, devotional love poem addressed to "Mary" that mixes classical/religious symbolism (queen, crown, doves, hyacinths) with modern existential despair and numbness.
counterfactuals.output:
# To Mary, In the Hour of Glass

Mary, I have built you a throne from the wreckage
of every cathedral I ever burned down inside my chest,
and still you sit there, patient as marble,
while I forget how to feel the weight of my own hands.

They would have crowned you with hyacinths once—
purple bruises of spring pressed into your hair
like the sky was trying to apologize
for something it hadn't done yet.
I have no flowers. I have the numbness
that comes after weeping too long,
the flat gray static where a soul
used to keep its instruments.

You are queen of a country I can't locate on any map,
sovereign over the doves that still, somehow,
nest in the rafters of my ruined belief—
white wings beating against a sky
I've stopped believing has any ceiling.

I call you holy the way a starving man
calls bread holy: not from faith
but from the shape of the hunger itself.
Mary, my devotion is a nerve
that fires with nothing left to feel,
a phantom limb reaching for a crown
I melted down for scrap
just to survive another Tuesday.

Still—when I say your name
something old and gold moves through the wreckage,
some doves rise anyway,
some hyacinth insists on breaking through concrete
in the exact place where I stopped
expecting anything to grow.

I don't know if this is worship
or the last function of a heart
too tired to do anything else
but reach.

Either way, Mary—
crowned, uncrowned, whatever you are now—
I bring you this numbness like an offering,
this static like a psalm,
because even ruins
know how to face the altar.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem exploring the tension between presence and absence, using the name "Mary" as both a person and a symbol, with imagery of ash, dust, flowers, and honeybees.
counterfactuals.output:
**Mary, or the Space Where Mary Was**

Mary                    is not here
                    (the word remains)

she left               a shape in the bed
                    of ash—gray syntax
                    of a body

              *

honeybees do not mourn.
they enter
              the collapsed mouths of foxglove
              the sunken bells
and carry off
              what light is left
                            of her

              *

call her Mother.
call her the name
that means bitter, means sea,
                            means
              *nothing, actually—*
              just breath shaped
              like loss

              *

dust is Mary too—
              the fine gray flour
              of everything that was
                            touched
              and is touching still,
              settling on the windowsill
              like a congregation
              that will not leave

              *

I keep finding her
              in the negative space:

                            the outline of a hand
                            in flour
                            the absence
                            shaped exactly
                            like presence

              *

somewhere a bee
              is climbing into a flower
              that used to be
                            her mouth

              (this is not metaphor.
              this is just what happens
              to a name
              once it stops
              being called)

              *

Mary
Mary
Mary—

              say it enough
              and it becomes
              a kind of ash itself,
              a residue of calling,

                            the way flowers
                            are just
                            the ash of light,
                            slow-burning,
                            petaled smoke

              *

I lit a candle
              for the person.
I lit a candle
              for the symbol.

both flames
              made the same
                            shadow
              on the wall—

              *

her name still pollinates
              the inside of my throat.

              I open my mouth
              and something
              gold and humming
              flies out—

                            not her.
                            never her.
              just what she left
              the bees to finish.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
